If a distance rule drops the 8-point neighbour, the standardized lag becomes (12 + 16)/2 = 14 percentage points. The change follows the neighbourhood definition, not a sudden economic movement. Inspect isolated locations and whether distance or contiguity matches the mechanism of interest. A higher lag does not prove neighbours caused D’s value; it only summarizes values under the declared weights. See “GeoDa Center — Global Spatial Autocorrelation workbook”.
spatial-dependence-regional-econometrics.Moran’s I summarizes global similarity a: Moran’s I is best read together with its null and weights matrix. In a synthetic five-region map, an observed I of 0.30 may look positive, but its meaning depends on which pairs are connected and how rows are standardized. If 24 of 999 random permutations produce I values at least 0.30, the one-sided Monte Carlo proportion with the usual correction is (24 + 1)/(999 + 1) = 0.025, or 2.5%. That is unusual under this fixed-location randomization, not evidence that one region transmitted unemployment to another. Repeat with a substantively defensible alternative neighbourhood rule and inspect local patterns separately; a global statistic does not identify the responsible cluster. See “PySAL esda — Global Spatial Autocorrelation with Moran’s I”.
spatial-dependence-regional-econometrics.Spatial lag and spatial error tell diffe: Separate an observed neighbour outcome from an unobserved shared shock. In a synthetic model, region output is 140 million currency units and its row-standardized neighbour outcome is 100 million. A lag coefficient of 0.4 contributes 40 million units before the intercept and other terms; this is a model component, not automatically a causal effect. Under a spatial-error story, the region might instead receive an unobserved 8-million-unit shock correlated with nearby shocks, with no observed neighbour outcome entering the equation. Simultaneity makes neighbouring outcomes endogenous, so ordinary least squares with that term is not a safe shortcut. Choose the model from timing, institutions, and identification, not from a map alone. See “PySAL esda — Global Spatial Autocorrelation with Moran’s I”.
spatial-dependence-regional-econometrics.Stress-test the geography and causal cla: A sensitivity table should show both the spatial rule and the statistic’s scale. In a synthetic residual analysis, contiguity gives Moran’s I = 0.31, a 50-kilometre band gives 0.18, and eight nearest neighbours gives 0.27. The largest difference is 0.13 index points, not 13 percentage points, because I is dimensionless. A stable positive sign supports a repeated descriptive association; the smaller value warns that strength depends on what “nearby” means. Also check whether one large region drives the result and whether residual dependence remains after covariates. None of these checks establishes rail-induced spillovers without an exposure definition, timing, comparison strategy, and interference assumptions. See “GeoDa Center — Global Spatial Autocorrelation workbook”.

bootstrap-inference.Resample the data you have: Replacement means a bootstrap replicate can repeat an observation while omitting another. For a synthetic sample of monthly profits $80, $100, $120, and $200, the observed mean is $125. One size-four replicate, $80, $80, $120, and $200, has mean ($80 + $80 + $120 + $200)/4 = $120. Another replicate can differ even though every draw comes from the same four recorded units. Across many replicates, the distribution describes variation conditional on this empirical sample. It does not add omitted firms, repair selection bias, or prove the population mean. If records are clustered by district, resample districts rather than rows. The sample and resampling unit must represent the collection design. See “Penn State STAT 555, §15.3 — Bootstrapping (sampling-distribution diagram)”.
bootstrap-inference.Read spread and intervals from the boots: The bootstrap lab reports two different summaries: Bootstrap SE of median is the sample standard deviation of the T* values, while the percentile interval uses their lower and upper quantiles. Suppose a synthetic set of five bootstrap medians is £18, £19, £20, £22, and £26 per hour. Their average is £21 per hour, but the standard deviation describes spread in pounds per hour, not percent. With only five replicates, tail quantiles are unstable; use many more repetitions before reading approximate 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. The trace should look stable as replicate number grows, and the histogram should reveal skew or boundary effects. Neither summary guarantees that a fixed population median lies inside the interval. See “NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook — Bootstrap Plot”.
bootstrap-inference.Match resampling to the data structure: The independent unit is determined by collection, not by spreadsheet layout. Synthetic example: three sampled districts each contain two wages: A has $12 and $14, B has $20 and $22, and C has $30 and $32. A district bootstrap draws three districts with replacement. Drawing A, B, and A yields six wages totaling $94, so the replicate mean is $15.67 per hour. Row-wise resampling could combine isolated workers from all districts and understate uncertainty when district conditions move together. For a time series, random rows also destroy order; blocks preserve local dependence. Record whether the design sampled people, districts, or time blocks before choosing a bootstrap. Repetitions cannot correct the wrong resampling unit. See “Angrist & Pischke (2009), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch. 8 — Nonstandard Standard Error Issues”.
bootstrap-inference.Choose a bootstrap model and inspect its: The bootstrap model determines which unobserved values are considered plausible. In a synthetic sample of delivery times 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7 minutes, a nonparametric replicate may repeat 3 and omit 7, producing 3, 3, 4, 6, 6 with mean 4.4 minutes. A fitted parametric model might generate 8 minutes, which is not in the sample but could be allowed by its assumed distribution. In the lab, inspect the Bootstrap trace for drift or unstable runs, then use the distribution histogram to assess skew, tails, and boundaries. A smooth trace from more repetitions does not validate the model. Report method, resampling unit, statistic, and limitations. See “NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook — Bootstrap Plot”.
bootstrap-inference.Connect bootstrap intervals to econometr: A confidence interval is only as credible as the resampling unit behind it. Suppose a synthetic policy is assigned to four districts, each containing 50 surveyed workers, and the estimated employment-rate difference is 3 percentage points. Resampling all 200 worker rows independently treats them as 200 independent assignments, which can make uncertainty too small. A district bootstrap draws four districts with replacement, carries along their workers, and recomputes the difference. The worker count describes outcomes, but the independent policy units are districts. With only four clusters, percentile limits may still be unstable. This synthetic calculation is not an empirical finding or causal proof; assignment validity and nonresponse remain separate assumptions. See “Angrist & Pischke (2009), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch. 8 — Nonstandard Standard Error Issues.”
bootstrap-inference.Apply it to a regional wage comparison: For a regional median comparison, keep the contrast identical through every replicate. Illustrative synthetic data give North wages of $10, $20, and $40 and South wages of $12, $14, and $16. The observed medians are $20 and $14, so North minus South equals $6 per hour. One bootstrap draw might repeat North’s $10, $40, $40, whose median is $40, and draw South’s $12, $12, $16, whose median is $12; that contrast is $28 per hour. Such a change is possible because each group is tiny, not evidence of a real wage shift. Read the replicate distribution as uncertainty about this sample contrast, while checking survey strata, weights, and nonresponse before using a simple bootstrap. The numbers are synthetic, not regional evidence. See “Hesterberg (2015) — What Teachers Should Know About the Bootstrap (open access).”

statistical-power-planning.Start with a decision-relevant causal ta: A planning target becomes testable only after its population, treatment contrast, outcome, and timing are fixed. Consider a synthetic training offer for eligible applicants, with weekly earnings measured 16 weeks after assignment. If the treatment mean is £260 and the control mean is £235, the difference is £25 per week, but that arithmetic is merely a proposed meaningful threshold, not a result. Changing the horizon or population changes the estimand. Individual assignment and centre assignment also answer different policy questions. Before using a power calculator, write the contrast in words and units, then state what randomization or adjustment is meant to identify it. Neither the £25 scenario nor its planned power guarantees a positive estimate or generalization. See “Cunningham, Causal Inference: The Mixtape, Ch. 4 — Potential Outcomes and Randomization.”
statistical-power-planning.Choose a precision target or a power tar: The same sample-size question can hide two different decisions. A precision plan asks how narrow an interval should be; a power plan asks how often a specified effect would cross a decision rule. Illustrative synthetic inputs for a one-mean precision calculation are a standard deviation of £120 and a desired 95% half-width of £30. The normal shortcut gives n ≈ (1.96×120/30)² = 7.84² ≈ 61.5, so one would round upward to 62 independent observations. That is not automatically the size for a two-arm difference, where both groups contribute variance. A power calculation would additionally specify a meaningful difference, alpha, and desired detection probability. Clustering, attrition, and non-normal outcomes can alter either result. The example is a planning scenario, not observed evidence. See “NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook — Sample Sizes Required for a Mean.”
statistical-power-planning.Distinguish power from the minimum detec: Minimum detectable effect is best read as a design threshold, not as a claim about what exists. Suppose a synthetic two-arm study has 80 independent people per arm, outcome standard deviation £160, a two-sided 5% test, and 80% target power. Using 1.96 + 0.84 = 2.80, the rough threshold is 2.80×√(2×160²/80). Since 160² = 25,600 and 2×25,600/80 = 640, the square root is about 25.30, giving an MDE near £70.84 per week. An estimated £40 difference could be important yet have less than the planned detection probability; failing to reject would not show zero effect. This shortcut assumes independent equal groups and a defensible standard deviation. If assignment is by centres, it is incomplete. The figures are synthetic, not a wage finding. See “Penn State STAT 509, Lesson 8 — Sample Size and Power.”
statistical-power-planning.Account for assignment, clustering and a: Recruitment inflation and information inflation are different problems. In a synthetic centre-based study, 12 centres each need 30 retained outcomes, giving a target of 360. With intraclass correlation 0.04, the design effect at m = 30 is 1 + (30−1)×0.04 = 2.16, so 360 retained observations represent about 360/2.16 = 166.7 independent-person equivalents. At expected attrition of 15%, recruit 360/(1−0.15) = 423.5, rounded up to 424. This aims to preserve the outcome count but does not create more than 12 independent centres; unequal retention changes cluster sizes and should prompt a revised design effect. Differential dropout can also change composition and bias a comparison. Report cluster count, cluster-size assumptions, correlation, attrition mechanism, and primary outcome together. These are illustrative calculations, not trial evidence.
statistical-power-planning.Power cannot repair a weak design: Precision can make a flawed comparison look certain. Imagine a synthetic programme in which participants earn £360 per week after enrolment and nonparticipants earn £330, a raw difference of £30. Suppose participants were already £18 higher before enrolment. A simple adjustment story would leave £30−£18 = £12, but that subtraction is not automatically valid: trends, selection, spillovers, and measurement may differ. Increasing the sample could shrink the standard error around either £30 or £12 while leaving assumptions untouched. Power calculations describe repeated-sampling performance under a model; they do not validate treatment assignment or establish potential outcomes. Diagnose the comparison first, then plan precision for the estimand the design can support. These values are synthetic and do not show a programme effect. See “Angrist & Pischke (2009), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch. 2 — The Experimental Ideal.”
statistical-power-planning.Plan a job-training evaluation: A useful evaluation plan exposes its uncertainty before data collection. Consider a synthetic design with six employment centres, 40 eligible applicants per centre, and anticipated attrition of 12%. It recruits 6×40 = 240 people and expects 240×0.88 = 211.2 observed outcomes, roughly 211 if fractional expectations are reported rather than rounded prematurely. If assignment is by centre, six independent assignments constrain inference more strongly than 240 rows suggest. A scenario table could evaluate weekly effects of £20, £40, and £60 under several plausible outcome standard deviations, rather than quietly choosing the most favourable input. State the outcome horizon, allocation rule, clustering, and missing-data plan. These are synthetic design calculations, not evidence that training changes wages, and power remains conditional on the assumptions. See “Penn State STAT 509, Lesson 8 — Sample Size and Power.”

measurement-error-economics.Name the concept and the recorded variab: Measurement begins before regression, when the analyst decides what the variable is supposed to mean. Suppose the target is usual weekly commuting time, but one synthetic respondent reports 35 minutes for four ordinary days and 75 minutes for an unusual trip. The five-day average is (35+35+35+35+75)/5 = 215/5 = 43 minutes, whereas a last-trip measure is 75 minutes. Neither number is simply “the commute” without a reference rule. The difference reflects definition and recall, not necessarily random noise. Record whether the unit is one-way or round-trip, whether transfers count, and which days are eligible. A validation route record could also measure a different concept. These figures are synthetic, not a labour-market finding. See “United Nations Statistics Division — Measurement Error in Household Surveys.”
measurement-error-economics.Classical predictor error can flatten a: The reliability ratio is a model-based multiplier, so calculate it only after checking its assumptions. In a synthetic single-regressor example, true commuting-time variance is 25 minutes² and independent reporting-error variance is 9 minutes². The ratio is 25/(25+9) = 25/34 ≈ 0.735. If the true slope were −£12 of monthly transport cost per additional minute, the expected slope using the noisy predictor would be 0.735×(−£12) ≈ −£8.82 per minute. The sign remains negative here, but the magnitude moves toward zero because unrelated noise enlarges observed predictor variance. This is not a universal correction: differential rounding, strategic reporting, omitted variables, and multiple regressors can change direction or interpretation. The numbers are synthetic and not evidence of a transport effect. See “Angrist & Pischke (2009), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch. 3 — Making Regression Make Sense.”
measurement-error-economics.Outcome error and non-classical error di: Ask which side of the regression carries the recording problem before predicting its consequence. Illustrative synthetic data have two training groups with true monthly earnings means of £2,200 and £2,700. In the first group, four outcome errors are −£80, +£40, +£20, and +£20; they sum to zero, so the recorded mean remains £2,200. In the second group, errors are −£100, +£50, +£25, and +£25, also summing to zero, leaving £2,700. The mean difference stays £500, although individual residuals become noisier. This illustration requires mean-zero errors within groups and a correctly specified comparison. If higher earners under-report systematically, the group means can move unequally. Outcome noise is not interchangeable with predictor error, and neither example establishes a causal training effect. See “United Nations Statistics Division — Measurement Error in Household Surveys.”
measurement-error-economics.Use data collection and validation to le: A validation exercise should specify its comparison target before collecting a second measure. Suppose a synthetic reinterview covers 12 people: first-reported weekly commuting totals 516 minutes and second reports total 492 minutes. The average second-minus-first difference is (492−516)/12 = −24/12 = −2 minutes per person per week. If a route-based record totals 504 minutes, its average is 42 minutes, while the first-report average is 43 minutes, a gap of 1 minute. These discrepancies can describe repeatability and disagreement, but they do not prove which source is correct. Route data may omit waiting, unusual trips, or unlinked journeys; reinterviews may share memory errors. Report coverage, timing, linkage, and sampling of the validation subsample. The numbers are synthetic, not survey evidence. See “United Nations Statistics Division — Measurement Error in Household Surveys.”
measurement-error-economics.Interpret a commuting-time regression ca: A coefficient’s units should be translated before its direction is discussed. In a synthetic regression, the estimated association is 0.6 minutes of reported one-way commuting per 1 percentage-point increase in a job-access score. Moving from 45 to 60 points is a 15-point change, so the fitted difference is 0.6×15 = 9 minutes, not 0.6 minutes. If responses are rounded to five-minute bands, treat the prediction as approximate: rounding can shift observations across bins, so nine minutes is not minute-level measurement precision. It remains conditional on the model and describes association: neighbourhood choice, job type, transport mode, and income may affect both access and commuting. Validation improves measurement, not control of those confounders. The calculation is synthetic and not a causal or historical result. See “Regression and Other Stories — authors’ book site and chapter resources.”

price-indices-real-values.An index summarizes a defined basket: The category weights in an index determine whose price experience is being summarized. Illustrative synthetic basket shares are 50% food, 30% housing, and 20% transport. If their price relatives are 1.10, 1.04, and 0.95, the weighted relative is 0.50×1.10 + 0.30×1.04 + 0.20×0.95 = 0.55 + 0.312 + 0.19 = 1.052. With a base of 100, the index is 105.2, meaning the specified basket costs 5.2% more than in the base period. It does not mean every household faced 5.2% inflation, and 105.2 is not a currency price. Check that weights sum to 1, categories are comparable, and the base and current prices share quality definitions. The values are synthetic, not official CPI data. See “U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — CPI Calculation.”
price-indices-real-values.Understand the base and the weights: A fixed-basket calculation makes normalization transparent. Consider a synthetic base basket of 5 meals at €10 and 10 transit rides at €2, costing €50 + €20 = €70. Later prices are €11 per meal and €1.80 per ride, so the same quantities cost €55 + €18 = €73. The Laspeyres index is 100×73/70 = 104.2857, or 104.3 rounded to one decimal place. The implied basket inflation is about 4.3%, while 104.3 is not €104.30. This result holds for the defined base quantities and quality; changed consumption, substitutions, or quality adjustments require care. Official indexes may use procedures beyond this classroom formula, so document the published methodology rather than treating the simple basket as universal. The example is synthetic, not official price evidence. See “Eurostat — Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices Methodological Manual (2024).”
price-indices-real-values.Calculate inflation from changes in the: Percentage change needs the starting index in the denominator. Suppose a synthetic transport index rises from 132 in January to 138.6 in April. The three-month rate is (138.6−132)/132×100 = 6.6/132×100 = 5%. The increase is 6.6 index points, but it is a 5% change, not 6.6% and not 138.6%. If a different city also moves from 132 to 138.6, the arithmetic matches only under compatible definitions, coverage, and timing; equal levels do not establish equal baskets. When reporting the result, name the interval and whether it is monthly, quarterly, or year-over-year. The calculation describes movement in the selected index, not its cause or a forecast. These numbers are synthetic, not regional inflation evidence. See “U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — Consumer Price Index: Concepts and Calculation.”
price-indices-real-values.Convert nominal values into real values: Deflation preserves the chosen base-period purchasing-power scale only when the numerator and deflator match in period and coverage. Consider a synthetic monthly stipend of £1,875 when the compatible price index is 125, with base 100. The real value is £1,875/(125/100) = £1,875/1.25 = £1,500 in base-period pounds. That does not mean the recipient receives £1,500 now; it is a comparison expressed in the base basket’s units. If the index instead were 120, the result would be £1,875/1.20 = £1,562.50, showing why deflator choice matters. Taxes, housing composition, quality, and household-specific spending remain outside this mechanical adjustment. The figures are illustrative and synthetic, not welfare evidence. See “U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — Consumer Price Index: Concepts and Calculation.”
price-indices-real-values.Compare pay with prices in an education: Real pay comparisons require matching the pay measure to a defensible price basket. Suppose a synthetic lecturer’s monthly salary rises from $4,000 to $4,160, a nominal increase of 4%. Over the same period, the selected education-worker price index rises from 100 to 106. The later salary in base-period dollars is $4,160/(106/100) = $4,160/1.06 ≈ $3,924.53. Relative to the original $4,000, the real-pay ratio is 3,924.53/4,000 ≈ 0.9811, a decline of about 1.9%. Subtracting 6% from 4% gives approximately −2%, close but not exact. The result concerns purchasing power under this index, not every lecturer’s household budget or a causal effect of inflation. The numbers are synthetic. See “Eurostat — Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices Methodological Manual (2024).”

regularization-cross-validation.Why a perfect historical fit can fail ne: Forecast evaluation must mimic the information available at the forecast date. Imagine a synthetic quarterly unemployment model trained through quarter 8 and evaluated on quarters 9–12. Predictions are 4, 6, 5, and 7 percentage points; actual changes are 5, 5, 6, and 6. Squared errors are 1, 1, 1, and 1, so test MSE is 1 and RMSE is 1 percentage point. Using later revisions or future indicators during preprocessing could report artificially low error because it leaked information. Randomly mixing future quarters into training folds creates a similar problem. Regularization may reduce coefficient instability, but cannot repair contaminated evaluation. These values are synthetic forecast arithmetic, not evidence about an agency or causal policy effect. See “James, Witten, Hastie, Tibshirani & Taylor — An Introduction to Statistical Learning (official free book site; linear-model regularization chapter).”
regularization-cross-validation.What Ridge and LASSO penalties change: Ridge and LASSO alter the optimization objective, so compare fit and penalty on the same scaled predictors. In a synthetic example, candidate A has RSS 9 and coefficients (0.7, −0.5); candidate B has RSS 10 and coefficients (0.3, −0.2), with λ = 1. Ridge objectives are 9 + 0.7² + 0.5² = 9.74 for A and 10 + 0.3² + 0.2² = 10.13 for B, so Ridge prefers A despite larger slopes. LASSO objectives are 9 + 0.7 + 0.5 = 10.2 and 10 + 0.3 + 0.2 = 10.5, again preferring A. A larger λ could reverse the choice, and LASSO may set coefficients to zero. Standardization must use training data only; selected variables are predictive choices, not causal discoveries. See “Cunningham — Ridge, LASSO, Elastic Net and Cross-Validation (course notes).”
regularization-cross-validation.Choose the penalty with cross-validation: Cross-validation is a comparison of prediction rules, so define the forecast information set before calculating scores. Illustrative synthetic example: a model predicts quarterly vacancy rates in percentage points using 16 earlier quarters, with four rolling validation origins. Candidate penalties have fold MSEs 0.81, 0.49, 0.64, and 0.36 for one setting, averaging 2.30/4 = 0.575 percentage-points-squared; its RMSE is √0.575 ≈ 0.76 percentage points. A second setting averages 0.64, so the first wins under squared loss. Scaling and imputation must be refit at every origin, and a final future block remains untouched. This is synthetic forecast arithmetic, not an unemployment result or causal estimate. See “James, Witten, Hastie, Tibshirani & Taylor — An Introduction to Statistical Learning (official free book site; linear-model regularization chapter).”
regularization-cross-validation.Read validation curves without chasing n: A tuning curve is most useful when its horizontal scale and uncertainty are visible. Suppose, illustratively, that log-penalties −3, −1, and 1 produce validation RMSEs of 2.41, 2.38, and 2.40 percentage points for the same forecast horizon. The middle value is numerically smallest, but the maximum difference is only 0.03 percentage points. If fold variation is larger, the ranking is fragile; choosing the more strongly penalized model may be reasonable if it uses fewer predictors and has nearly equal error. That choice should be reported as a stability or simplicity decision, not as proof that the stronger penalty is true. Compare every candidate with a baseline and preserve the test set. These are synthetic scores, not observed economic outcomes. See “Cunningham — Ridge, LASSO, Elastic Net and Cross-Validation (course notes).”
regularization-cross-validation.Keep prediction separate from economic e: A variable can be excellent for forecasting while being unsuitable for an intervention claim. Consider an illustrative synthetic model that predicts next-month electricity demand from weather, calendar indicators, and a utility’s past discount code. If the code improves forecast accuracy, it may proxy for expected demand or operational planning; its selected coefficient does not reveal what demand would be under a new discount policy. The relevant causal question requires a counterfactual assignment design, not merely a nonzero LASSO coefficient. Keep feature selection inside training data, describe the prediction target and horizon, and reserve causal language for a design that supports it. The example is constructed and neither predicts real demand nor estimates a policy effect. See “James, Witten, Hastie, Tibshirani & Taylor — An Introduction to Statistical Learning (official free book site; linear-model regularization chapter).”

meta-analysis-evidence-synthesis.Start with a question and a study-select: A review protocol should make an estimate eligible because it answers the target question, not because its sign is attractive. Suppose the target is the effect of a job-search offer on monthly earnings in dollars, measured six months after assignment, among unemployed adults. An illustrative report gives a four-month earnings effect, another gives six-month earnings, and a third gives a six-month standardized wellbeing score. The second matches the target; the first needs a prespecified separate category or exclusion, and the third is not interchangeable without a defensible conversion. Record search dates, eligible designs, population, comparison, outcome units, and follow-up. A pooled number cannot repair mismatched estimands. These examples are synthetic. See “Chabefer — Statistical Tools for Causal Inference, Chapter 13: Meta-analysis and Publication Bias.”
meta-analysis-evidence-synthesis.Weight estimates by precision, not by si: Inverse-variance weighting rewards smaller standard errors under a fixed-effect model, but it does not certify study quality. Illustrative synthetic estimates of a common wage change are Study A = $12 per month with SE $3 and Study B = $20 with SE $6. Their weights are 1/3² = 1/9 and 1/6² = 1/36, so A receives four times B’s weight. The pooled value is [(1/9)×12 + (1/36)×20] ÷ [(1/9)+(1/36)] = (48/36+20/36)/(5/36) = 68/5 = $13.60 per month. This arithmetic assumes a shared effect and comparable definitions. A precise but biased design is not rescued by its weight, and significance is not a weighting rule. See “Haghnejad & Farahati (2024) — An Overview of Meta-Analytic Methods for Economic Research (open preprint).”
meta-analysis-evidence-synthesis.Allow effects to vary across settings: Random-effects weighting changes the question from one common effect to an average across a distribution of settings. Take two illustrative synthetic estimates of annual earnings change: Study A is $80 with SE $8 and Study B is $140 with SE $16. If between-study variance is τ² = 256 dollars squared, the weights are 1/(64+256) = 0.003125 and 1/(256+256) = 0.001953125. The pooled mean is (0.003125×80 + 0.001953125×140)/(0.005078125) ≈ $103.1. Without τ², the first study would receive four times the second study’s weight; with it, the ratio is 1.6. The average is not guaranteed for a new labour market, and τ² itself is estimated. See “Haghnejad & Farahati (2024) — An Overview of Meta-Analytic Methods for Economic Research (open preprint).”
meta-analysis-evidence-synthesis.Explain heterogeneity without overfittin: Meta-regression treats studies, not participants, as observations. Suppose five evaluations report employment effects by programme length. A fitted +1.5-percentage-point contrast between 10- and 6-week programmes corresponds, under a linear moderator, to 1.5 ÷ (10−6) = 0.375 points per additional programme week at study level—not an individual dose response. Studies differ in populations and design, so that slope does not predict any participant’s gain from adding a week. If one evaluation contributes four outcomes from the same sample, treating them as four independent studies exaggerates information unless dependence is modeled or one outcome is prespecified. Five studies also limit moderator count. Report study count, dependence handling, and exploratory status. Synthetic values do not show that longer programmes cause employment gains. See “Chabefer — Statistical Tools for Causal Inference, Chapter 13: Meta-analysis and Publication Bias.”
meta-analysis-evidence-synthesis.Check what the published evidence leaves: Funnel asymmetry is a prompt to investigate, not a mechanical correction. Illustrative synthetic evidence contains eight small studies with SE 0.25 and eight large studies with SE 0.08. Seven small studies report positive effects, while four large studies do. The positive shares are 7/8 = 87.5% and 4/8 = 50%, a 37.5-percentage-point difference. Selective publication could create that pattern, but small studies might also use different populations, weaker designs, or genuinely different interventions; random variation is another possibility. Do not convert the contrast into a probability that studies are missing, and do not count positive papers as votes. Register search rules, seek unpublished evidence, inspect study features, and report sensitivity analyses. These numbers are synthetic, not a publication-bias estimate. See “Chabefer — Statistical Tools for Causal Inference, Chapter 13: Meta-analysis and Publication Bias.”

causal-mediation-mechanisms.Ask what pathway a mechanism claim propo: A mechanism claim needs more than a mediator that changes after treatment. Consider a synthetic tutoring offer, weekly practice minutes as M, and a certification outcome as Y. If offered learners practice 30 minutes more on average and certify more often, the diagram may propose T→M→Y, while also allowing a direct T→Y path. Motivation can point to both M and Y, so the practice difference alone is not a causal pathway estimate. First state the total treatment contrast and timing; then explain what intervention on the mediator would mean. Conditioning on a post-treatment variable can alter the target or open bias. The diagram organizes assumptions, not findings. This example is constructed and does not show a tutoring effect. See “Imai, Keele & Tingley — A General Approach to Causal Mediation Analysis.”
causal-mediation-mechanisms.Separate total, direct and indirect effe: The coefficient-product shortcut is a model-specific decomposition, so keep units attached to every path. In an illustrative additive linear model, an offer increases mentoring sessions by a = 0.8 sessions per person, and one additional session corresponds to b = 3 percentage points of certification; the direct path is c′ = 2 percentage points. The indirect path is ab = 0.8×3 = 2.4 percentage points, and the total is c′+ab = 4.4 percentage points. These values are constructed, not observed. The arithmetic requires the stated linear, additive specification and mediation identification assumptions. With a treatment–mediator interaction or a nonlinear binary outcome, direct and indirect effects must be defined through counterfactual predictions instead of assumed to add this way. See “Imai, Keele & Yamamoto (2010) — Identification, Inference and Sensitivity Analysis for Causal Mediation Effects.”
causal-mediation-mechanisms.See why treatment randomization is not e: Randomization answers the offer-versus-no-offer question, not automatically the question of receiving a particular mediator level. Suppose a synthetic experiment assigns 150 people to coaching and 150 to control. Employment is 54% versus 48%, a total-assignment difference of 6 percentage points. Within coaching, highly motivated participants attend eight sessions and less motivated participants attend three; motivation also predicts employment. The eight-versus-three comparison is therefore confounded even though the offer was randomized. Sequential ignorability requires stronger control of mediator–outcome confounding, plus defensible timing and overlap. Adjustment for a measured baseline factor may help but cannot certify that no unmeasured factor remains. The percentages are synthetic and do not identify a coaching mechanism. See “Imai, Keele & Yamamoto (2010) — Identification, Inference and Sensitivity Analysis for Causal Mediation Effects.”
causal-mediation-mechanisms.Match estimation to the outcome and desi: Always identify the outcome scale before interpreting a mediation path. In a synthetic binary completion example, predicted probability rises from 0.35 under no offer to 0.41 under an offer. The difference is 0.06 probability units, or 6 percentage points; relative to 0.35 it is 0.06/0.35 ≈ 17.1%, a different statement. A logistic coefficient is measured in log-odds, so multiplying a treatment-to-mediator coefficient by a mediator coefficient does not automatically produce six percentage points. With interactions, calculate specified counterfactual predicted probabilities under the relevant treatment and mediator settings. Check measurement order, overlap, and the confounding assumptions before calling that contrast causal. These values are synthetic predictions, not completion data. See “Imai, Keele & Tingley — A General Approach to Causal Mediation Analysis.”
causal-mediation-mechanisms.Use sensitivity analysis and report the: Sensitivity analysis is a map of what conclusions require, not a detector for the hidden confounder. Suppose an illustrative mediation calculation gives an indirect effect of 3.2 percentage points when the bias parameter is zero. Under a hypothetical confounding scenario, the adjustment is −0.9 points, giving 3.2−0.9 = 2.3 points; under a stronger scenario, the adjustment is −3.2, giving 0.0 points. Report the parameter’s meaning, units, range, and whether the total effect changes. If a plausible scenario reaches zero, describe the pathway as assumption-sensitive rather than robust. Do not present these scenarios as measured bias or empirical outputs. Separate evidence for the overall treatment effect from evidence for the proposed mediator. See “Imai, Keele & Yamamoto (2010) — Identification, Inference and Sensitivity Analysis for Causal Mediation Effects.”

partial-identification-bounds.Replace an implausibly exact answer with: A set-valued answer is often the honest result when an unobserved quantity is only constrained. For an illustrative synthetic hourly wage effect θ, suppose the available design and assumptions imply −$1.50 ≤ θ ≤ $4.50. The identified set is [−$1.50, $4.50], with width $6 per hour. It rules out a $7 effect, but it does not assign equal probability to every value inside the set and does not justify calling the midpoint, $1.50, the estimate. If a policy requires at least $2 per hour, the data alone do not establish that the threshold is met because values below $2 remain compatible. The range concerns the stated population and outcome scale; it is not automatically causal or a confidence interval. See “Tamer (2010) — Partial Identification in Econometrics, Annual Review of Economics.”
partial-identification-bounds.Derive worst-case bounds for missing bin: For a binary outcome, calculate each group’s full mean range before subtracting groups. In an illustrative synthetic six-month repayment study, 85% of offered borrowers respond and 64% of responders repay. Their full-group mean lies in [0.85×0.64, 0.85×0.64+0.15] = [0.544, 0.694]. Among controls, 75% respond and 56% of responders repay, giving [0.75×0.56, 0.75×0.56+0.25] = [0.420, 0.670]. The treatment-minus-control effect is therefore [0.544−0.670, 0.694−0.420] = [−0.126, 0.274], or −12.6 to +27.4 percentage points. The sign remains unresolved. These are worst-case population-style calculations under binary support, not a confidence interval or observed repayment effect. See “Huntington-Klein — The Effect, Chapter 21: Partial Identification.”
partial-identification-bounds.Tighten bounds only with assumptions you: A narrower bound is informative only after its narrowing restriction is made visible. Suppose 70% of a synthetic treatment group responds and the observed success share is 0.50. Unrestricted binary outcomes give [0.70×0.50, 0.70×0.50+0.30] = [0.35, 0.65]. Now suppose external validation defensibly limits the missing group’s success probability to 0.20–0.60. Its contribution is 0.30×[0.20, 0.60] = [0.06, 0.18], producing [0.41, 0.53]. The width falls from 0.30 to 0.12, or from 30 to 12 percentage points, because some missing-outcome worlds were excluded. That restriction is not learned automatically from the observed arm; compare alternatives and label the result conditional. The figures are synthetic. See “Tamer (2010) — Partial Identification in Econometrics, Annual Review of Economics.”
partial-identification-bounds.Keep identified sets and confidence inte: Two kinds of uncertainty can coexist. An identified set describes which population effects remain compatible with the assumptions, while sampling uncertainty describes how estimated endpoints would vary across samples. Illustratively, a sample calculation yields [0.10, 0.34] in probability units for a 12-month outcome, a width of 0.24 or 24 percentage points. That width is not a standard error. If a separate resampling analysis suggests endpoint variability around 0.03 units, it still does not follow that [0.07, 0.37] is automatically a valid confidence region; the two endpoints may be dependent and require an appropriate inference procedure. The teaching interval is not a confidence interval unless its construction is specified. These values are synthetic, not lab or survey results. See “Huntington-Klein — The Effect, Chapter 21: Partial Identification.”
partial-identification-bounds.Report what the range can and cannot rul: Interpret an identified set by checking its sign, scale, and policy thresholds. Suppose a synthetic evaluation of a binary employment outcome at nine months gives [−0.02, 0.15]. In percentage-point language, that is −2 to +15 percentage points: both slight harm and substantial benefit remain compatible, so the sign is unresolved. The set rules out a 20-percentage-point increase because 0.20 exceeds the upper endpoint. Its midpoint is (−0.02+0.15)/2 = 0.065, or 6.5 percentage points, but that is only a descriptive centre unless a separate model justifies it. Report missingness, assumptions, population, timing, and endpoint method; do not turn the range into a conventional null-test conclusion. The numbers are synthetic. See “Tamer (2010) — Partial Identification in Econometrics, Annual Review of Economics.”
